question: A design review for a customer-support agent that can read tickets, issue refunds and email customers lists these decisions. Assess each one.

rows.text: Remove the account-deletion tool, which support staff never need, instead of guarding it with a confirmation step.
rows.note: Least privilege: a capability the agent does not hold cannot be misused.

rows.text: Rely on a system-prompt line telling the agent to ignore instructions found inside customer emails as the main injection defence.
rows.note: Prompt instructions are one layer, not a control. Limit what a manipulated agent can do.

rows.text: Require human approval before any refund above a set amount is executed.
rows.note: Irreversible, high-impact actions get a gate before they happen, not an audit after.

rows.text: Log only the final reply to save storage, since intermediate tool calls rarely matter.
rows.note: Multi-step failures happen at intermediate steps; trace every step under one request ID.

rows.text: Treat text returned by tools and retrieved documents as untrusted data rather than instructions.
rows.note: Untrusted content belongs in tool results and must not be able to trigger sensitive actions on its own.

rows.text: Give the agent one shared admin account so it can always reach every customer record.
rows.note: Act with the user's scoped identity; a shared admin account lets any user reach anything through the agent.

explanation: The pattern across all six: put controls in architecture (tool scope, gates, identity, tracing) rather than in prompt wording.

question: Match each query pattern to the retrieval approach that fits it best.
choices: Whole corpus in the prompt with caching

rows.text: Support questions that often contain exact error codes such as E-4021 and product SKUs.
rows.note: Embeddings miss exact identifiers; BM25 catches them. Combine both.

rows.text: "What was the total refund amount by region last quarter?"
rows.note: Aggregations over structured data need a query, not semantic search over rows.

rows.text: Q&A over a 70,000-token policy handbook that changes once a quarter.
rows.answer: Whole corpus in the prompt with caching
rows.note: Under roughly 200k tokens Anthropic suggests skipping RAG and caching the whole corpus.

rows.text: Questions that need facts from several documents in a large repository that changes daily.
rows.note: Let the agent search, read and iterate just in time instead of one lookup.

rows.text: A mix of conceptual questions and questions naming specific internal product names.
rows.note: Semantic search handles the concepts, lexical search the exact names.

explanation: Match the retrieval method to the data shape and the query pattern; no single method fits every case.

question: A client has a zero data retention (ZDR) arrangement with Anthropic. For each Claude API feature, is it ZDR-eligible?

rows.text: Prompt caching
rows.note: Prompts and outputs are not stored; only KV cache representations and hashes, briefly.

rows.text: Message Batches API
rows.note: Results are retained for 29 days for asynchronous retrieval.

rows.text: Files API
rows.note: Files are kept until deleted or until they expire.

rows.text: Code execution tool
rows.note: Container data is retained for up to 30 days.

rows.text: Web search tool
rows.note: Results are returned in the API response.

rows.text: Agent Skills
rows.note: Skill data follows the standard retention policy.

explanation: Stateful features that store jobs, files or containers cannot be zero-retention. Using one is a choice to step outside ZDR for that data.

question: Choose the pattern that best fits each requirement.

rows.text: Inbound requests fall into four known, distinct categories that each need different handling.
rows.note: Classify first, then send each category to a specialised prompt or model.

rows.text: Marketing translations must follow a precise glossary and tone guide, and first drafts keep missing terms.
rows.note: There is a clear rubric, and a check-and-revise loop measurably helps.

rows.text: A long report has fixed, independent sections that can be drafted at the same time to cut latency.
rows.note: Fixed subtasks decided in code, run concurrently.

rows.text: A research task whose subtasks depend on what the input turns out to contain.
rows.note: A lead model decides the split at run time and delegates it.

rows.text: Insurance claims of three labelled types, each with its own set of checks.
rows.note: Known categories with labelled history make routing cheap and accurate.

explanation: Pick by what is known at design time: categories (routing), a rubric (evaluator-optimizer), fixed independent parts (sectioning), or input-dependent subtasks (orchestrator-workers).

question: A platform team is rolling Claude Code out to 200 developers. Choose the mechanism for each requirement.

rows.text: No developer may let Claude read .env files, and nobody can override it locally.
rows.note: Managed settings sit at the top of precedence, and a deny there cannot be allowed elsewhere.

rows.text: Run the formatter automatically after every file edit.
rows.note: A PostToolUse hook runs deterministically every time.

rows.text: Describe the project's coding conventions and test commands for Claude to follow.
rows.note: Guidance the model weighs, shared through the repository.

rows.text: A multi-step release procedure that is needed only a few times a month.
rows.note: Progressive disclosure: only the description loads until the skill is used.

rows.text: Inspect each shell command's arguments with custom logic and block risky ones before they run.
rows.note: A PreToolUse hook can deny the call with custom logic before it executes.

explanation: Enforcement goes in settings or hooks, guidance in CLAUDE.md, and occasional procedures in Skills.

question: For a remote MCP server protected with OAuth, mark each statement true or false according to the MCP authorization specification.

rows.text: The server must verify that each access token was issued for this server as its audience.
rows.note: Audience validation per RFC 8707 is a MUST.

rows.text: The server may forward the client's access token to a downstream API to save a token exchange.
rows.note: Servers must not accept or transit tokens not issued for them; pass-through enables confused-deputy attacks.

rows.text: Clients may put the access token in the URL query string if the Authorization header is inconvenient.
rows.note: Tokens must not be sent in the query string.

rows.text: A local server using the stdio transport should take credentials from the environment rather than run the OAuth flow.
rows.note: The spec says stdio implementations should not follow the HTTP authorization flow.

rows.text: Clients must send the resource parameter identifying the MCP server in authorization and token requests.
rows.note: Resource indicators are required in both requests.

explanation: The spec's core protections are audience-bound tokens, no token pass-through, and tokens only in the Authorization header.

question: For each use, decide whether a qualified human must review the output before it reaches or affects the person, under GDPR Article 22 or Anthropic's high-risk use requirements.

rows.text: Declining an EU consumer's loan application.
rows.note: A solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effect needs human intervention and a way to contest.

rows.text: Tagging inbound support tickets by product area.
rows.note: Low-impact internal routing; monitor quality.

rows.text: Giving an individual a recommendation about their legal situation.
rows.note: Legal is a high-risk area: a qualified person reviews, and the person is told AI was used.

rows.text: Summarising internal meeting notes for the attendees.
rows.note: No decision about an individual.

rows.text: Recommending whether to approve a job applicant.
rows.note: Employment is a high-risk area, and the decision significantly affects the person.

explanation: Human review attaches to decisions that significantly affect a person or fall in a high-risk domain, not to every automated step.
